prompt: Which of these are valid polynomial-time many-one reductions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Independent Set to Vertex Cover: keep the graph and subtract the requested independent size from the vertex count
options.explanation: Valid. A set is independent exactly when the remaining vertices form a cover.

options.text: Independent Set to Clique: complement the graph and retain the target size
options.explanation: Valid. Independent sets of G are cliques of the complement graph, built with one check per pair of vertices (about n²/2 for n vertices).

options.text: 3-SAT to IS: enumerate every assignment with brute force; then output a fixed yes-instance or no-instance
options.explanation: The yes/no result is preserved, but enumerating all assignments is exponential in the variable count, so the stated construction is not a polynomial-time reduction.

options.text: Vertex Cover to Set Cover: use edges as elements and one incident-edge set per vertex, retaining the budget
options.explanation: Valid. Some k vertices touch every edge exactly when their k sets cover every element.

options.text: Subset Sum to Unary Subset Sum: rewrite each number in unary
options.explanation: Invalid. A number written in b bits can be as large as about 2 to the power b, and unary encoding needs that many symbols, so the output is exponentially larger than the input.

workedExample:
Check each against the two rules: (i) polynomial time, (ii) yes-instances map to yes-instances and no-instances to no-instances. The notation used in the options:

```formula
(G, k) ↦ (G, n − k)
(G, k) ↦ (Ḡ, k)
L_unary ≈ 2^b
L_unary ≈ 1.8 × 10^19   for b = 64
where
↦: "maps to": the instance on the left is turned into the instance on the right
G: the input graph
k: the target size in the input instance
n: the number of vertices of G
Ḡ: G-bar, the complement graph: same vertices, edges exactly where G has none
b: the number of bits used to write a number in binary
L_unary: the length of the same number written in unary (one symbol per unit), up to about 2 to the power b symbols; 2^64 is about 1.8 × 10^19
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the first two maps only rewrite the target number or flip the edges, which is fast. Unary turns a 64-bit number into up to about 1.8 × 10^19 symbols, exponentially longer than the input.
```

1. Independent Set to Vertex Cover: trivially fast; correct by the complement identity.
2. Independent Set to Clique: about n²/2 steps to build the complement; correct by the complement-graph identity.
3. 'Solve, then output a fixed instance' satisfies (ii) but not (i). If it ran in polynomial time you'd have shown P equals NP already.
4. Edges-as-elements: fast; correct, since covering an edge means picking one of its endpoints.
5. Unary encoding: output size exponential in input size, violates (i). (Unary subset sum is in P by the DP; that's consistent.)

prompt: A paper claims "SCHEDULE is NP-complete" with this proof: (1) a schedule is a certificate checkable in polynomial time; (2) we give a polynomial-time reduction from SCHEDULE to 3-SAT. What has actually been proven?

options.explanation: Step (2) is in the wrong direction. A reduction from SCHEDULE to 3-SAT says 3-SAT can solve SCHEDULE, which is true for every NP problem.

options.text: Only that SCHEDULE is in NP
options.explanation: Correct. Step (1) proves membership in NP, and step (2) adds nothing new, since everything in NP reduces to 3-SAT by Cook–Levin. NP-hardness needs a reduction the other way, from 3-SAT to SCHEDULE.

options.text: SCHEDULE is NP-hard but maybe not in NP
options.explanation: Nothing in the argument establishes hardness.
No algorithm for SCHEDULE has been given; reducing to 3-SAT gives only an exponential-time algorithm (via brute-force SAT).

workedExample:
1. Read the reduction symbol carefully:

```formula
A ≤_p B
SCHEDULE ≤_p 3-SAT
3-SAT ≤_p SCHEDULE
where
≤_p: "polynomial-time reduces to": a polynomial-time translation maps every instance of the left problem to an instance of the right one with the same yes/no answer, so the right problem is at least as hard as the left
A, B: any two decision problems
SCHEDULE: the paper's scheduling problem
3-SAT: satisfiability of formulas made of clauses with 3 literals each; known to be NP-complete
In words: a reduction from A to B shows B is at least as hard as A. The paper proved the second line (SCHEDULE reduces to 3-SAT), which only says 3-SAT is at least as hard as SCHEDULE. Hardness of SCHEDULE needs the third line.
```

2. That direction is true for every problem in NP anyway (Cook–Levin plus the reduction from SAT to 3-SAT), so it proves nothing new.
3. Needed: a reduction from 3-SAT to SCHEDULE, showing SCHEDULE is at least as hard as 3-SAT.
4. So only step (1) carries weight: SCHEDULE is in NP.
5. Mnemonic: reduce *from* the known hard problem *to* the new one.

prompt: Many-one (Karp) versus Turing (Cook) reductions. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Under Turing reductions, UNSAT reduces to SAT trivially: call SAT once and negate the answer
options.explanation: Correct. Turing reductions may post-process the oracle's answer, so complements are free.

options.text: If UNSAT many-one reduces to SAT in polynomial time, then NP equals coNP
options.explanation: Correct. A Karp reduction would put UNSAT in NP; UNSAT is coNP-complete, so every coNP problem would be in NP, and hence NP and coNP would be equal.

options.text: NP-completeness is standardly defined using Karp reductions
options.explanation: Correct. Using Turing reductions would make NP and coNP problems equally 'complete', erasing a distinction we believe is real.

options.text: A Turing reduction may call the target problem at most once
options.explanation: That's the many-one restriction. Turing reductions may make polynomially many adaptive calls.

options.text: Karp reductions are more powerful than Turing reductions
options.explanation: Backwards. Every Karp reduction is a Turing reduction with one call and no post-processing, so Turing reductions are at least as powerful.

workedExample:
1. Karp (many-one): one query, answer passed through as is.
2. Turing: an algorithm for A that may query B many times and do anything with the answers.

```formula
A ≤_p B
x ∈ A  iff  f(x) ∈ B
where
≤_p: "polynomial-time (Karp) reduces to": the second line holds for a polynomial-time f; written ≤p in the options
A: the problem being reduced (here UNSAT)
B: the problem it is reduced to (here SAT)
x: any instance of A
f: the Karp reduction: a polynomial-time algorithm turning an instance of A into an instance of B
f(x): the instance of B built from x
∈: "is a yes-instance of"
In words: a Karp reduction maps yes-instances to yes-instances and no-instances to no-instances, with no chance to flip the answer afterwards.
```

3. 'Negate SAT's answer' is a one-query Turing reduction from UNSAT to SAT, but not a Karp one.
4. A Karp reduction from UNSAT to SAT would give: φ is unsatisfiable exactly when f(φ) is satisfiable. A satisfying assignment for f(φ) is then a short certificate of unsatisfiability, so UNSAT would be in NP:

```formula
UNSAT ∈ NP  gives  coNP ⊆ NP
coNP ⊆ NP  gives  NP = coNP
where
UNSAT: the set of Boolean formulas with no satisfying assignment; it is coNP-complete
NP: the class NP (nondeterministic polynomial time): decision problems whose yes-answers have a short certificate checkable in polynomial time
coNP: the class coNP: decision problems whose no-answers have short, polynomial-time-checkable certificates (complements of NP problems)
∈: "is a member of"
⊆: "is contained in": every problem in the left class is also in the right class
In words: if UNSAT had short yes-certificates, every coNP problem would too, and NP and coNP would collapse into one class, which is conjectured false.
```

5. That's why the finer Karp notion is used to define NP-completeness.
